extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students of poetics/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic drama (especially tragedy): its nature as imitation, the necessary parts of a tragedy, and rules for constructing plot, character, diction, and other elements to produce pity, fear, and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation (three differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (and related arts) are modes of imitation which differ in three respects—the medium, the objects, and the manner (mode) of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medium: rhythm, language, harmony (singly or combined). Objects: types of people/actions represented (better, worse, or as in life). Manner: narration or presentation (characters acting before us). Use this tripartite distinction to choose form (epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, etc.) and to decide how to imitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the work imitates an action (not merely character or speeches), uses elevated language and musical elements where appropriate, and aims to arouse pity and fear leading to emotional purgation. Tragedy should be enacted (dramatic), not merely told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality—Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot = arrangement of incidents (the soul of tragedy); Character = qualities by which agents are known; Diction = metrical arrangement/wording; Thought = where things are proved or general truths enunciated; Song = chief embellishment among the embellishments; Spectacle = least artistic element (dependent on stagecraft). Evaluate and compose with priority: Plot > Character > Thought > Diction > Song > Spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as primary (arrangement of incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy; it is the imitation of the action and consists in the arrangement of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize constructing a coherent, causally linked sequence of incidents. A string of well-crafted speeches or lifelike character portrayals cannot substitute for a properly constructed plot. The most powerful tragic effects (peripeteia, recognition) are parts of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and wholeness of plot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning is that which does not follow anything by causal necessity; an end is that which follows nothing; a middle follows and is followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the plot has a natural beginning, middle, and end; events must follow by probability or necessity. The plot's magnitude must be such that the sequence of events can be grasped in one view (memory/representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (one action only)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot, being an imitation of an action, must imitate one action; the structural union of parts should be such that removing any part disjoints the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to include all episodes of a hero's life; center the play on a single, unified action whose parts are organically necessary to that action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding epeisodic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots—where episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence—are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble loosely connected episodes for show; ensure causal/probable connections bind incidents into a single, coherent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude/length appropriate to perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty depends on magnitude and order. The proper magnitude is one which can be embraced in a single view; neither too small nor too vast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a span (traditionally about a single revolution of the sun for tragedy) that allows the audience to apprehend the unity and sequence; avoid plots so long that the eye/memory cannot take them in at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plots should be probable or necessary (not mere accident)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry represents what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity; the poet relates what may happen, not merely what happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents should be credible and arise from causal or probable connections rather than pure coincidence. Even surprises should have an air of design—events should feel like necessary or probable consequences of preceding incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either Simple (change of fortune without Reversal or Recognition) or Complex (change accompanied by Reversal of the Situation and/or Recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the complex form for a perfect tragedy—use reversal and recognition arising from the plot's internal structure rather than external contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to probability or necessity (e.g., messenger who comes to cheer but reveals the opposite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reversals that arise naturally from preceding actions. A reversal should produce a meaningful change in direction of the action and contribute to pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; the best form coincides with Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognitions (discovery of identity, truth of actions) that are intimately connected with the plot; strongest when combined with reversal to produce emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action such as death onstage, bodily agony, wounds and the like—one of the parts of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes of suffering judiciously when they serve the plot's causal logic and the production of pity/fear; they are part of the complex action where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect should arise from internal structure, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but they should result from the inner structure of the piece; producing the effect by mere spectacle is less artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the plot's design and the incidents' arrangement to evoke emotions. Spectacle is ancillary and the least artistic element; avoid leaning on stage tricks to create the proper tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper protagonist type (neither wholly virtuous nor villainous)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should not be the fall of a virtuous man to misfortune (which shocks but arouses neither pity nor fear) nor the rise of a bad man; rather it should be of a man 'between'—not eminently good and just, nor utterly depraved—whose misfortune is brought about by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a central figure who is highly reputed and prosperous but falls through error (hamartia) or frailty; this elicits pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (relatability). Avoid extremes that fail to produce the tragic emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should aim to arouse pity and fear and effect catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates actions which inspire pity and fear; by these emotions it effects the proper purgation (catharsis) of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose incidents, reversals, recognitions, and character choices to generate pity and fear in an audience, aiming at their emotional purge rather than mere shock or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal; the poet makes plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is more philosophical and higher than history because it expresses the universal (what a person of a certain type would do) while history reports particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing, focus on actions that reveal general truths about types of persons; the poet's primary role is to invent and craft plots (not merely versify historical record). Names are secondary to actions that exemplify universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/structural parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exode, parode, stasimon, commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into Prologue (precedes Parode), Episode (between choric songs), Exode (no choric song after it); Choric parts: Parode (first utterance of Chorus), Stasimon (choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters), Commos (joint lamentation of Chorus and actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these formal divisions to organize the play's flow. Each part has conventional placement and function; structure the plot so episodes and choric odes interrelate coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Thought defined and prioritized
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words (metrical arrangement); Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent—where something is proved or a general maxim is enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speeches so that diction (wording/metre) and thought (arguments, maxim, proof) serve the action and reveal purpose. Thought should make choices and intentions manifest; diction should convey meaning fittingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as chief embellishment; Spectacle as least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Among embellishments Song holds the chief place; Spectacle has emotional attraction but is least artistic and connected least with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate choral/song elements as essential embellishment of the poetic art, but do not elevate spectacle over the poetic devices that produce tragic effect; stagecraft should support, not substitute for, poetic construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of traditional material with invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may use received legends (house-histories) but should show invention of their own and skilfully handle traditional material; they need not slavishly stick to received names/topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use traditional myths as material when they contain moving incidents suited to tragedy, but exercise inventive restructuring to imprint the tragic quality; the poet is free to alter particulars to better realize probable/universal actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer single-issue plots over double threads for true tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue, rather than double; double-thread (two catastrophes) pleases weak spectators but is not the true tragic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single, coherent catastrophic movement (typically good-to-bad) as the central issue of the tragedy rather than splitting emotional focus across opposing outcomes.
